title: Shabari's fruit
hookLine: an old woman of the forest who waited years for one visit
carry: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, offered with love
last: AS YOU ACT, SO YOU BECOME.

cards: On the western shore of Lake Pampa there's a hermitage that has outlived its teachers. The sages who lived there, disciples of the great rishi Matanga, have all left this world.

One person stayed behind: an old woman, an ascetic, living alone among the trees. Before they went, her teachers told her that Rama would come one day, and that she should wait for him. She has been waiting a long time.

teach.b: Her name is Shabari. Valmiki calls her a shramani, a woman ascetic, and some readers hear in her name the Shabaras, a forest people.

When the brothers arrive, she rises, bows at their feet, and welcomes them the way the old texts describe: water for their feet, water to rinse the mouth, a seat. Rama asks what you'd ask any respected elder.
Has your practice gone well? Have you mastered anger? Is your mind at peace?
She answers, in effect: today my practice has borne fruit, because I've seen you. She has gathered forest fruits for him, and she offers them. Look at who is honoring whom.
Rama is a prince of Ayodhya. Shabari is an old woman alone in the forest, with no rank at all. And the prince sits in her hermitage and receives what she gives.
This is bhakti, loving devotion, and Shabari is one of its great examples: no rank, no fame, only love and long practice, and that's enough.

teach.h: BHAKTI: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says it outright: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with love, I accept.
It's why Hindu families place food before God first, an offering called naivedya, and then share it as prasad, a blessing.

teach.h: THE TASTED BERRIES: A LATER TELLING.
teach.b: Then there's the story told in many homes: Shabari tasted each berry first, so only the sweet ones went to Rama. It isn't in Valmiki; it grew in later tellings, songs and sermons.
But it says the same thing: what matters is the love in the offering.

how: Shabari is honored as a model of devotion (bhakti) that needs no rank or learning; families offer food to God first (naivedya) and share it as prasad, and the berry story is told in later Ramayanas, songs and sermons.

o: the forest ascetic who waited a long time for Rama
the queen who raised Rama in the palace of Ayodhya
a forest goddess who guards Lake Pampa's shore

games.q: at Matanga's hermitage — tap the pairs.
p: the rishi whose students taught her
food offered to God before anyone eats

s: in Valmiki, Shabari tastes the berries before giving them to Rama
that story comes from later tellings; Valmiki has her offer fruits she gathered.
Shabari was told by her teachers to wait for Rama
they left this world and told her Rama would come.
Rama asks Shabari about her practice and her peace of mind
he speaks to her as to a respected elder.

games.q: your little cousin is worried her mandir offering is too small: one banana. what do you tell her?
o: save up and bring something nicer next time.
a leaf, a flower, a fruit, offered with love, is enough.
offerings only count when a priest makes them.
games.why: Shabari had no rank and offered forest fruit, and Rama took it gladly; in the Gita, Krishna accepts what's offered with love.

practice: If you have a home shrine, or even a quiet shelf, place one small thing there: a flower, a piece of fruit, a glass of water. Offer it with the simplest thought: this is for you.
If you don't pray, give it to someone in your home instead, with the same care. Then sit a moment with Shabari's patience, ready, without needing to know when.

wordCard.voice: Shabari. The forest ascetic who waited at Matanga's hermitage, and offered Rama the fruit she'd gathered, with love.

orig.note: Sanskrit śabarī: the name of the ascetic at Matanga's hermitage, which some readers link to the Śabara, a forest people.

carryVoice: Your line: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, offered with love. Tomorrow, more time with Shabari. That's day five hundred seventy-eight.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 73–74 (Matanga's hermitage; Shabari welcomes Rama)
